takeaway: Dynamic Merkle Trees reshape themselves around skewed block accesses, shortening authentication paths for hot data and making integrity-protected cloud NVMe disks faster and more capacity-scalable.
background: Merkle trees authenticate current disk contents for confidential VMs whose memory is trusted but attached storage is not. Every verified read or durable update follows hashes to a protected root, providing freshness against corruption, relocation, and replay.
villain: Balanced trees give every block the same path length, so capacity growth adds hashes even though real storage workloads repeatedly touch a small working set. On fast NVMe, serialized SHA-256 updates—not metadata I/O—can dominate the data access, and high fanout hashes more bytes per node.
approach: The paper maps an optimal hash tree to a Huffman prefix code weighted by block-access probability, then approximates it online with Dynamic Merkle Trees. DMT probabilistically splays a cached leaf's parent by a hotness-derived distance, preserving leaf/internal-node roles and recomputing authenticated paths after rotations.
impact: DMT supplies integrity and freshness while adapting to changing access skew without an advance trace. It establishes that workload-shaped, unbalanced authentication structures can outperform static balanced Merkle trees, though they spend extra memory and storage on explicit links and counters.

evaluation.overview: AWS experiments sweep capacity, cache size, skew, read ratio, I/O size, threads, and queue depth, then replay an Alibaba volume trace and run Filebench OLTP; metrics include throughput, median/tail latency, and metadata overhead.
evaluation.implemented: About 5 KLOC of C++ implements binary, 4-, 8-, and 64-ary trees, an offline Huffman-optimal oracle, and DMT as Linux userspace block drivers through BDUS, with AES-GCM, keyed SHA-256, an LRU hash cache, and immediate verification/update.
evaluation.setting: AWS EC2 i4i.8xlarge instances with 32 cores, 256 GB memory, and local NVMe devices; fio workloads use five-minute warmups and 15-minute measurements across capacities through 4 TB, followed by Alibaba trace replay and a 922-GB ext4 OLTP dataset.

results.text: Under the write-heavy Zipf(2.5) workload, DMT maintains more than 85% of offline-optimal throughput across tested capacities and reaches 2.2× the balanced binary tree's throughput at 4 TB.
On the evaluated Alibaba cloud-volume trace at 4 TB, DMT is 1.3× faster than the balanced binary tree; on Filebench OLTP it improves read and write throughput by 1.8× and 1.7×.

DMT incurs 0.44×/0.80× additional in-memory metadata for leaf/internal nodes and 0.29×/0.75× additional storage metadata, but beats binary trees using one-tenth their cache ratio in a reported comparison.

limitations: The AWS instances do not support confidential-VM technology, so the prototype models trusted memory rather than running inside such a VM. Benefits rely on access skew: uniform access costs about 6% versus a binary tree and can favor balanced 4-/8-ary trees. Updates still use a global tree lock; DMT requires explicit metadata; and the study targets NVMe rather than HDDs.
phd_group_signal: The paper derives a systems design from an information-theoretic optimum, measures the true bottleneck before optimizing, and tests sensitivity plus real traces. It is a useful bridge among storage security, adaptive data structures, caching, and workload analysis.

claims.text: For independent accesses with known probabilities, constructing the Merkle tree as a Huffman prefix tree minimizes the expected number of hashes on an authentication path.
DMT samples one percent of accesses by default for splaying and uses cache-resident hotness counters to promote frequently accessed regions while amortizing rotation and rehashing cost.
